lead: Correlative coding, also called partial response signalling, deliberately adds a small known intersymbol interference so that a binary stream can fit a realisable Nyquist filter. M-ary PAM takes the other route to higher speed: it sends log₂M bits on each symbol by using M amplitude levels. Duobinary is the standard example: cₖ = aₖ + aₖ₋₁ gives three levels at the Nyquist bandwidth. These ideas appear in wireline modems, digital subscriber lines, and high-speed serial links where the ideal sinc pulse cannot be built.
prereq: You need: 5.1 and 5.2 for Nyquist bandwidth and pulse shaping; 5.6 for the error probability formula extended to M levels.

blocks.text: A Nyquist pulse with zero ISI needs a sinc spectrum, which is flat to R_s/2 and then zero. A real filter cannot make that sharp edge. Correlative coding accepts a small, known ISI instead. The simplest scheme is duobinary, or class I partial response. Its coder adds each symbol to the previous one: cₖ = aₖ + aₖ₋₁. If aₖ is 0 or 1, cₖ takes three values: 0, 1, 2. The symbol rate is still R_s, and the required bandwidth is R_s/2, so the bit rate per hertz is 2 bit/s/Hz. That equals the ideal binary Nyquist rate, now with a gradual, realisable filter.

A direct duobinary receiver must subtract the previous decision to recover aₖ. One wrong decision then corrupts every later bit. The precoder removes that memory. Before the coder, form pₖ = bₖ ⊕ pₖ₋₁, where bₖ is the input bit, pₖ is the precoded bit, and ⊕ is XOR. Start with p₀ = 0 (one bit of memory held in the precoder) before the first input bit b₁. The coder sends cₖ = pₖ + pₖ₋₁. The receiver decides the three levels and then applies b̂ₖ = cₖ mod 2. Because (pₖ + pₖ₋₁) mod 2 = pₖ ⊕ pₖ₋₁ = bₖ, the decode uses only the current level. A single level error gives one bit error, not a burst.

items: Precode each input bit with one bit of memory: pₖ = bₖ ⊕ pₖ₋₁, starting from p₀ = 0.
Add the precoded bit to its delayed copy: cₖ = pₖ + pₖ₋₁.
Send the three-level symbols through the Nyquist channel.
Slice at two thresholds, midway between 0 and 1 and between 1 and 2.
Decode each decided level modulo 2: b̂ₖ = cₖ mod 2.

blocks.text: cₖ = pₖ + pₖ₋₁,   b̂ₖ = cₖ mod 2
blocks.where: cₖ is the three-level channel symbol at time k; pₖ is the precoded binary symbol; b̂ₖ is the recovered bit; mod 2 gives the remainder after division by 2.

blocks.text: Duobinary has a DC component because its levels 0, 1, 2 are not symmetric. Modified duobinary uses cₖ = aₖ − aₖ₋₂. The delay is two symbols, and the subtraction gives levels −1, 0, 1 when aₖ is 0 or 1. The DC term cancels, which suits transformer-coupled lines and some magnetic recording channels. In delay-operator notation, duobinary is 1 + D and modified duobinary is 1 − D², where D means one symbol delay.

Duobinary gives up noise margin. Binary PAM has one threshold; duobinary has two thresholds and three levels. At the same average transmitted power its adjacent levels sit closer together than binary's, and its 1 + D receive filter also passes more noise than an ideal Nyquist filter. Its error probability is therefore much higher than ideal binary at the same power — far more than a factor of two at high SNR — a real SNR penalty. The gain is a realisable filter at bandwidth R_s/2, not extra bits per symbol. One input bit still produces one three-level symbol.

M-ary PAM sends log₂M bits on each symbol by using M amplitude levels. Binary PAM is M = 2; 4-PAM has four levels and sends two bits per symbol. The symbol rate falls for the same bit rate: R_s = R_b / log₂M. With a raised cosine filter of roll-off α, the bandwidth is B = (R_s/2)(1 + α). The receiver needs M − 1 decision thresholds, placed midway between adjacent levels.

Space the M levels as ±d, ±3d, ..., so the gap between neighbours is 2d. The average symbol energy is E_avg = (M² − 1)d²/3. For binary PAM this gives d², and for 4-PAM it gives 5d². If you keep the same gap d and raise M, the average symbol energy becomes (M² − 1)/3 times the binary value, so the power cost grows with the square of M.

Use Gray labelling: assign bit patterns so that neighbouring levels differ in only one bit. Then a noise spike that moves the decision to the next level usually causes one bit error, not several. The error probability for M-PAM still follows the nearest-neighbour idea from 5.6: it depends on the distance between adjacent levels and on N₀.

blocks.where: R_s is symbol rate in baud; R_b is bit rate in bit/s; M is the number of PAM levels; α is the raised cosine roll-off, 0 ≤ α ≤ 1; B is the required bandwidth in Hz.
E_avg is the average symbol energy; M is the number of levels; d is half the spacing between adjacent levels, with levels at ±d, ±3d, ...

figure.caption: The precoder breaks the error-propagation loop; the coder turns one bit into three levels, and the receiver slices two thresholds and takes the level modulo 2.

spec.title: Duobinary transmitter and receiver
spec.aria: The binary stream is precoded with one bit of memory, added to its own delayed copy to make three levels, sent over the channel, decided with two thresholds, and decoded by taking the level modulo two.

examples.question: A link must carry 9600 bit/s with a raised cosine roll-off α = 0.25. Compare binary PAM and 4-PAM: find the symbol rate, the 4-PAM symbol duration, the bandwidth, the number of decision thresholds, and the average-energy penalty for the same level spacing.
steps: Binary PAM: log₂2 = 1 bit per symbol, so R_s = 9600/1 = 9600 baud. Bandwidth B = (9600/2)(1 + 0.25) = 4800 × 1.25 = 6000 Hz. Thresholds = M − 1 = 2 − 1 = 1.
4-PAM: log₂4 = 2 bits per symbol, so R_s = 9600/2 = 4800 baud. Symbol duration T = 1/4800 = 208.33 µs. Bandwidth B = (4800/2)(1 + 0.25) = 2400 × 1.25 = 3000 Hz. Thresholds = M − 1 = 4 − 1 = 3.
Average energy for the same spacing d: binary E_avg = (2² − 1)d²/3 = d². 4-PAM E_avg = (4² − 1)d²/3 = 15d²/3 = 5d². The ratio is 5.
Power penalty in decibels: 10 log₁₀(5) = 6.99 dB, about 7 dB.
examples.answer: Binary PAM uses 9600 baud, 6000 Hz and one threshold; 4-PAM uses 4800 baud, 208.33 µs per symbol, 3000 Hz and three thresholds, costing 5 times (about 6.99 dB) average energy for the same spacing.
examples.check:
import math
Rb = 9600.0
alpha = 0.25
M2 = 2
M4 = 4
Rs_bin = Rb / math.log2(M2)
B_bin = (Rs_bin / 2) * (1 + alpha)
th_bin = M2 - 1
Rs_4 = Rb / math.log2(M4)
T4_us = 1e6 / Rs_4
B_4 = (Rs_4 / 2) * (1 + alpha)
th_4 = M4 - 1
ratio = (M4**2 - 1) / (M2**2 - 1)
pen_db = 10 * math.log10(ratio)
print(Rs_bin)
print(B_bin)
print(th_bin)
print(Rs_4)
print(round(T4_us, 2))
print(B_4)
print(th_4)
print(ratio)
print(round(pen_db, 2))

traps: Running duobinary without a precoder: the receiver must subtract the previous decision, so one wrong three-level decision corrupts every later bit.
Decoding duobinary by taking cₖ mod 3 or by subtracting the previous level: with the precoder the correct decode is simply b̂ₖ = cₖ mod 2.
Thinking duobinary's three levels carry more bits per symbol: one binary input bit still produces one three-level symbol; the gain is a realisable Nyquist filter.
Using M thresholds for M-ary PAM: there are M − 1 thresholds. Also remember the power penalty (M² − 1)/3 for the same spacing, so lower bandwidth is not free.
Mixing duobinary 1 + D with modified duobinary 1 − D²: the minus sign removes the DC component and uses a two-symbol delay.

quiz.q: What are the three possible output levels of the duobinary coder when the precoded input pₖ is binary 0 or 1?
quiz.a: The coder output is cₖ = pₖ + pₖ₋₁, so the levels are 0, 1 and 2.

quiz.q: Why is a precoder placed before the duobinary coder?
quiz.a: Without it, the receiver must subtract the previous decided bit, so one wrong decision propagates. With pₖ = bₖ ⊕ pₖ₋₁, the decoder is b̂ₖ = cₖ mod 2, which uses only the current level. One level error causes one bit error.

quiz.q: A binary source sends 64 kbit/s through 8-PAM with raised cosine roll-off α = 0.5. Find the symbol rate and the bandwidth.
Duobinary has three levels and binary PAM has two, yet both reach 2 bit/s/Hz. Explain how duobinary does this.
quiz.a: Duobinary still sends one input bit per symbol at rate R_s, so its bit rate is R_s. The coder adds a controlled ISI that shapes the spectrum to fit a gradual filter of bandwidth R_s/2. Binary Nyquist needs the same bandwidth but with an ideal sinc filter. Duobinary reaches 2 bit/s/Hz with a realisable filter, not by sending more bits per symbol.

quiz.q: For 16-PAM, how many bits per symbol and how many decision thresholds are there?
quiz.a: Bits per symbol = log₂16 = 4. Decision thresholds = M − 1 = 15.

quiz.q: A 16-PAM system has levels spaced 2d with d = 0.5 V. Find the average symbol energy and the number of thresholds.
Why does Gray labelling help in M-ary PAM?
quiz.a: Gray labelling makes neighbouring levels differ in only one bit. Most errors move the decision to an adjacent level, so one symbol error usually causes one bit error. Without Gray labelling, the same symbol error could flip several bits.

beyond: Not for the exam. Partial-response ideas reappear in partial-response maximum-likelihood (PRML) detectors for magnetic and optical storage, where a Viterbi detector handles the deliberate ISI instead of a simple slicer. DSL and high-speed serial links use precoding and PAM to approach the Nyquist rate over twisted pair or backplane channels. Modern 400G Ethernet uses PAM4, which sends two bits per symbol and needs half the symbol rate of binary for the same bit rate. Search for PRML, duobinary precoder, Tomlinson-Harashima precoding and PAM4 eye diagrams.
